references.text: The fourth commandment in the Decalogue, which commands keeping the Sabbath holy and resting on the seventh day, just as God rested after creation.
Command to work for six days and rest on the seventh day, with the same structure as in 35:2.
Parallel text containing the same death penalty for working on the Sabbath, describing the Sabbath as holy to the Lord.
Repetition of the Sabbath commandment focusing on six days of work and rest on the seventh day.
The Sabbath is described as a holy assembly where no work shall be done, a שַׁבַּת שַׁבָּתוֹן.
Example of enforcement of the death penalty for working on the Sabbath, where a man was stoned for gathering wood.
Restatement of the Sabbath commandment in Deuteronomy with theological justification based on deliverance from Egypt.
The prophet Ezekiel refers to the Sabbath as a sign between God and Israel, given so that they would know that the Lord sanctifies them.
Hebrews speaks of a Sabbath rest (σαββατισμός) awaiting God's people, linking it to God's rest after creation.
Direct parallel from the same law text confirming the death penalty for breaking the Sabbath.
The ethical constitution (Ten Commandments) providing context for the specific penal provision in Exodus 35.
Immediate contextual explanation of why the Sabbath is holy and the consequence of desecration.
Deuteronomy's repetition of the Ten Commandments confirming the inclusive character of the Sabbath for the entire community.
The historical introduction of the Sabbath in the wilderness showing God's practical provision to observe the commandment.
